en: A Dharma discourse on the method of the descent of the pen by the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, delivered by an old monk of Nanhai to the faithful: "I have made a vow to universally deliver all worldly beings; for this reason, there is the Heart Sūtra."

This tradition has been transmitted for a very long time. Those who merely recite it by mouth have become increasingly muddled, while those who force interpretations have fallen into the trap of the wild foxes.
Thus, the single-minded intention to deliver both humans and devas has been reduced to the doctrines of karmic retribution and the Lesser Vehicle; this is truly a matter for deep compassion.

May the late Master Lü, the Ancestor of our Way, explain each word and phrase, ruthlessly sweeping away all fragmentation and returning [the teaching] to its clarity. This is my aspiration for the Way.
Lamp. Relying upon it, [the light] shall not be extinguished. Excellent, excellent!

If worldly people can faithfully uphold this with confidence, their bodies will possess radiance, they will be protected by auspicious deities, they shall not fall into saṃsāra, nor descend into the realms of suffering. The myriad seeds of transgression will be entirely eliminated.
I pray that you expedite its publication so that all may universally achieve wholesome fruits.
The Great Compassion Mantra verses:
White lotuses are fragrant and lush; purple bamboos are verdant and flourishing. The seven afflictions break through obscurations, and wisdom dispels ignorance.
One awakens to the true emptiness of the five aggregates, and the four fruits of realization merge in harmony. The sun rises over the sea.
Ciyong: This verse was bestowed by the Great Being through his brush on the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the Xinchou year of the Daoguang era, saying:
"The old monk has specifically revealed this verse of the Great Compassion Mantra for you to adorn the Great [Buddha]."
The Compassionate Mantra. This is the opening verse of the *Heart Sūtra*. For all those of good faith who recite this gāthā with sincerity, there will be great spiritual resonance.
It should be widely propagated and chanted; its merit is as described in the *Shougui Lun* (Treatise on the Gathering of Merit). I have now respectfully transcribed and added it here for publication.
I hope that all followers of the Dharma will reverently supplement their recitations and circulate it far and wide; the resulting blessings and virtues shall be immeasurable.
The Heart Sutra,
annotated by Lord Fu-yu (Fu Yu Di Jun) and revised for re-engraving by the Daoist Zhen Jin-yi Pei.
The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom [Note]:
Prajñā means wisdom. Pāramitā means "reaching the other shore. Ta means concentration. Sūtra means path.
It is said that this sutra is the path for stabilizing the mind.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
It delivers one from all suffering and distress. Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Śāriputra, the empty nature of these dharmas is neither born nor destroyed;
it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases. Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no...
There is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. There is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomenon.
There is no realm of the eye, and so forth, up to no realm of consciousness. There is no ignorance, nor is there the extinction of ignorance;

and so forth, up to no old age and death, nor is there the extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path. There is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas (pronounced yùn), by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have minds free from hindrance.
Because they are free from hindrance, they have no fear; they are far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, and they attain ultimate Nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore...
Know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great spiritual mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, an unequaled mantra.
It is able to eliminate all suffering; because it is true and not false, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken.
Thus the mantra is recited: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi*.
*Tathāgata* [Note]:

Avalokiteśvara means that transformation proceeds from the mind; it is the attainment of insight through self-realization. *Bodhi* means awakening (*bodhana*). *Sattva* means sentient beings (*sattva*).
Since the principle is primordially complete, one is able to awaken to the meaning of all sentient beings. It signifies being stored within. Form, sensation, perception...
Volitional formations and consciousness—these are called the five aggregates. This single phrase is emphasized throughout the entire sutra.
"To deliver one from all suffering and distress" refers both to delivering oneself and delivering others. Śāriputra is a personal name. Because of form, there is sensation;

because of sensation, there is perception; because of perception, there are volitional formations; when volitional formations do not find their outlet, they are registered in the mind as consciousness and are not forgotten. These are the five.
They are mutually dependent. As for the empty characteristic of all dharmas, it refers to the true nature (*tathatā*). It exists yet is not existent; it is non-existent yet is not non-existent.
This is the empty characteristic of all dharmas. Because the true nature is not destroyed throughout kalpas, it is neither born nor extinguished.
Because the true nature is originally undefiled, it is neither defiled nor pure. Because the true nature does not cling to a single thing, it neither increases nor...

Subtracting [the previous categories], there are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharma*); these are called the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
All phenomena arise conditioned by the mind; therefore, phenomena belong to the mind. Some say that "dharma" is synonymous with "fa," meaning "to initiate" or "to set in motion.
Furthermore, this term also applies to what is seen by the eyes as the "eye-element" (*cakṣur-dhātu*), and to where the mind goes as the... [mind-element].
The consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*). "Without ignorance" means there is no state of delusion or obscurity. "Without old age and death" means it exists eternally and is indestructible.
"Suffering" (*duḥkha*) refers to affliction. "Origin" (*samudaya*) refers to accumulation; it is as if saying that ten thousand transgressions are accumulated within a single body.
These two are called the fruit of suffering and the cause of suffering. "Cessation" (*nirodha*) is *nirvāṇa*. "Path" (*mārga*) is the way; it is as if saying...
This is the path attained through practice. Second is what is called the "fruit of bliss" and the "cause of bliss.
In Sanskrit, it is *bodhisattva*; in the language of China, it is *púsà*. *Nir* means "not born"; *vāṇa* means "not dying. *A* means "non-existent"; *nuttara* means "supreme. Third.
*Samyak* means "correct. *Sambodhi* means "perfect enlightenment. *Gatye gatye* means "to the [noble] truths";
it is repeated to signify both saving oneself and saving others. *Saṃgha* means "the assembly.
*Svāhā* means "speedily," signifying the swift accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings.
[Commentary] Ānanda said: "In my teaching, there is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, whose meritorious practice is most profound and who possesses great wisdom.
When he reached the further shore, he perceived that both his own five aggregates and the five aggregates of sentient beings are all empty and void.
Regarding himself, he cultivated unsurpassed bodhi; regarding others, he [acted] in manifold ways..."
He received them and led them in, so that all their afflictions and calamities might be entirely brought to liberation.
The disciple Śāriputra was one who truly sought to escape from suffering and calamity. The Bodhisattva called him by name and addressed him, saying:
"Śāriputra, you know that whatever in the world has form is 'form' (rūpa), and whatever is formless is 'emptiness' (śūnyatā). Yet you do not realize that form is like a dream or an illusion."
Bubbles and shadows are no different from emptiness; emptiness is the manifestation of the one true reality, and it is no different from form.
Is form not itself emptiness? Is emptiness not itself form? Because of form there arises sensation; because of sensation there arises perception;
because of perception there arise mental formations. When these formations cannot be attained, consciousness dwells within the mind and does not forget them. This...
Fifth, these are seen as being mutually dependent. Now, since form is itself emptiness, so too are sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Because this true nature is eternally pure and eternally serene, there is not the slightest dharma-characteristic by which it can be named;
is this not truly the characteristic of emptiness among all dharmas? To speak of its subtlety: it exists eternally without obstruction, and is unarisen.
It is not extinguished; it is profoundly still, pure, and void. It is neither defiled nor pure. It is spontaneously perfect, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Therefore, within true emptiness, since there are no form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, the six sense organs are all pure, lacking eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The six sense objects do not disturb it, and there is no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon.

This is the Dharma. Among the afflictions of the six sense organs, the eye is primary. Now that the visual field is empty, all external conditions are extinguished and the mental consciousness is entirely forgotten.
Thus, one will see that from concentration comes stillness, and from stillness comes wisdom; there is no longer ignorance.
Nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance. Through long duration it becomes firm; through firmness it becomes steadfast.

There is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death. These are the bitter fruit of afflictions, the causal basis for the suffering of karma, and the joyful fruit of nirvana.
When the causes for the joy of cultivation are simultaneously exhausted, then within true emptiness there is fundamentally no wisdom to be named;
even reaching the other shore belongs to the realm of the provisional and false—so what could possibly be attained? Thus, there is neither wisdom nor attainment.
This is spoken from the perspective of after one has already attained Bodhi. If it were prior to its attainment, could there possibly be no Dharma?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva takes the Prajñāpāramitā as the method of practice;
by guarding the six sense faculties and severing the six sensory objects, the mind is free from entanglement and obstruction, remaining far removed from [all defilements].
The inversion of the spirit and mind, the deluded thoughts of dreams and sleep—these persist until one reaches the state of neither birth nor death.

This is true not only for Bodhisattvas; even the Buddhas of the three periods of time, desiring to attain unsurpassed bodhi, have none who do not rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā. Thus we know that the Prajñāpāramitā...
This is the esoteric teaching of unfathomable transformation; this is the esoteric teaching of universally illuminating divine light;
this is the esoteric teaching of the ultimate beyond compare; this is the esoteric teaching of peerless and solitary excellence.
What Ānanda has said—that it can eliminate all suffering—is truly real and not false. Furthermore, there is an esoteric mantra which you should recite from time to time.
By this, one can give rise to wisdom and reach the other shore. The mantra says: *gate gate pāragate*.
"Gate" means to bring forth the wondrous truth (*miao-di*) in order to deliver others; it is repeated to signify delivering oneself and delivering others. "Pāragate" means reaching the other shore.
To reach the other shore, one must rely upon this sublime truth. *Saṃgha* means "the assembly. *Svāhā* means "speedily";
it refers to the swift accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings. In short, although the secret mantra is the path of practice, that path does not exist apart from this mind.
If a person can empty the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), then they are the master.
When one is constantly settled in samādhi, adventitious sensations naturally clear away; how could there be anyone who fails to attain unsurpassed bodhi?
Mei examined the Heart Sūtra and found that reading it in six sections makes it clear:
from "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" to "crosses over all suffering and distress" constitutes one section; from "Śāriputra" to "neither ignorance nor attainment" constitutes another section.
From "By means of non-apprehension" to "reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*" constitutes one section.
From "The Buddhas of the three periods of time" to "thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" constitutes one section.
From "Therefore know that the *prajñāpāramitā*" to "therefore it is called the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra" constitutes one section. Then he spoke the mantra, saying: [the mantra follows].

*Bodhi svāhā*. This constitutes one section. Although the original scripture was composed as a single, continuous flow, dividing it into these six sections is like observing ripples upon the surface of flowing water;
it makes the initial reading easier to comprehend. [This concludes] the final section.
One should place the character "also" (又) beneath the character "that" (即) to explain it. This sutra emphasizes the characters "one" (一) and "many" (多).
Without "many," one cannot achieve success.
*The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (Concluded).
The general purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is essentially to cause people to guard the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and sever the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

That these six faculties and six objects are impure is because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have not yet been emptied. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva specifically brought this out to demonstrate it.

For later students, this serves as the path for returning to the ultimate source. The text consists of only two hundred and sixty-eight characters, yet its words are concise while its meaning is comprehensive;
it can encompass the entirety of the thirty-two sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One may read the *Vajracchedikā* without reading the *Heart Sūtra*, but...
This is to wander into the vast without knowing how to return to the concise. Alas!
How can this be? A respectful postscript by Chunyangzi, appended to the first chapter of the thirty-two gāthās from the descent of the Grand Master Lü.
Once you have attained the skillful hand, do not harbor doubt; if doubt arises, you will lose your way on the path.
Walking straight forward, ascend the mountain peak; there, the willows are lovely and the flowers are radiant—encountering them is naturally wondrous.
Chapter Two.
Doing good is like climbing a hundred-foot pole; It is easy to come down, but difficult to climb up.
One must exert diligent effort regarding merits and faults; The difference between human and beast is slight—this requires careful reflection.
(Chapter Three)
The swift passage of time cannot be halted; year after year we see only the waters flow eastward.
If you do not believe this, try holding up a green water-lily to reflect yourself: that former crimson countenance is now white-haired.
Chapter Four.
Ten thousand turns, the body like an unmoored boat— When winds toss it and waves surge, it is hard to retrieve.
Holding fast to the oar and rudder at the stream’s edge, With a light sail along the way, one reaches the shore.
Chapter Five.
All phenomena are empty; do not seek them in vain. The Tathāgata resides only within this very mind.
Cast away the shackles of attachment and the fetters of craving; Without grasping and without constraint, one attains freedom.
Chapter Six.
How many varieties of heavenly bliss are there? Yet for souls bound by craving, it is difficult to emerge from the prison of suffering.
Suffering and joy have always been a matter of a single thought; The blue lotus was originally planted amidst boiling water.
Chapter Seven.
The bonds of affection and love cannot be untied; When one day the body departs, they can no longer be shared.
Now, casting them off with no lingering attachment, One ascends directly to the Jade Terrace of Mount Ling.
Chapter Eight.
Wealth and nobility have always been like bubbles upon the water; why need one ride a crane to Yangzhou?
In the Lotus Pond there is a method for gathering the mind: within stillness, one often chants "Seven Strokes Struck Through.
Chapter Nine.
Flowers fall and flowers bloom once more in another year; how many times in human life does one see the moon ever full?
Having unfastened the shackles of fame and profit, amidst the surging flames, it is best to plant the lotus.
Chapter Ten.
The mind and its objects must always be cleared away, Do not allow afflictions to invade you daily.
On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa lies infinite leisure; By the side of the Pond of Merit, wash away the six defilements.
Chapter Eleven.
Cease allowing the six thieves to attack daily; All forms and colors are entirely empty.
Realize that originally there is not a single thing; The numinous terrace resides only within this very mind.
Chapter Twelve.
To seek the path outside the mind is to go astray; The moon’s reflection in water, flowers in a mirror—do you know the wondrous meaning of true emptiness?
Adorned with the seven treasures, all is ultimately suboptimal.
Chapter Thirteen.
Wherever the wind and banner move, it is all not the truth; This very mind is the sovereign suchness.
If you can understand the meaning of the plucking of the flower and the smile, Where could even a speck of dust originally find a place to settle?
Chapter Fourteen.
The fleeting light of time passes swiftly; do not let it slip away.

Bound and entangled by fame and profit as if caught in a net, there is no other method than to cast off your hands at the edge of a precipice and pay homage to Amitābha beside the white lotus pedestal.
Chapter Fifteen.
Busily occupied day after day with worldly affairs, One mistakenly takes the path of delusion for one’s true home.
If you recognize your original, true countenance, You will see this body is but a stinking skin-sack.
Chapter Sixteen.
After the Lantern Festival, there are no more lanterns; The gate of ten thousand ages is always this very mind.
Shining brightly upon all heavens, it never extinguishes; A single shrine of Buddha-fire through three watches of the night.
Chapter Seventeen.
Seeing beauty as if it were non-existent, keep the mind focused on the One; do not entice others with resentment toward the Māra-dancing girls.
Guard against female form as you would against a thief; how then could external invaders seize the master?
Chapter Eighteen.
Beside the Terrace for Gazing at Home, one still longs for family; The moon is bleak and the wind mournful as the dark path slants away.
Though there be paper money, there is nowhere to use it, All because that single thought was mistaken.
Chapter Nineteen.
In the Hall of the Forest of All Things, ghosts appear in myriad forms; There are cauldrons of boiling oil and mountains of ten thousand blades.
If one realizes the true meaning of the Tathāgata, Boundless liberation is attained all at once.
Chapter Twenty.
Trapped and immersed for many years, The river of craving flows vast, its waves reaching the heavens.
By upholding this sutra, one may ascend to the high bank; What need is there for a boat further upon the middle current?
Chapter Twenty-One.
Once worldly attachments are severed, they naturally dissolve; Only through purity does one realize that form is emptiness.
The Buddha is the mind, and the mind is the Buddha; The green mountains are always within the white clouds.
Chapter Twenty-Two.
I have heard it said that in the West, various lotuses grow; Their blossoms open ten fathoms high, with stalks as large as boats.
Within the Hall of the Spirit, there naturally exists the Jeta Grove tree; The splendor of one’s original ground is itself the Buddha-heaven.
Chapter Twenty-three.
The coquettish girl was originally but a powder-smeared skull;
though she had no worries over evening pleasures and morning joys, once impermanence leads her back to the path of the underworld, she can no longer display her former charms in the night realm.
Chapter Twenty-Four.
To pile up treasures into mountains is not truly marvelous; It is not as good as upholding this sutra to attain Bodhi.
This Golden Sutra clearly reveals the true path; Why weep over lost sheep at the fork in the road?
Chapter Twenty-Five.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are this very mind; Why need they be molded from clay or gilded with gold?
Those in the world who light candles and burn incense— They make the Compassionate Avalokiteśvara laugh to tears.
Chapter Twenty-Six.
Awakening is like finding a lamp in the night; A windowless, dark room suddenly becomes bright.
If this body is not saved within the sutras, Where else shall one find salvation for this body?
Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Eliminating evil is like disentangling a tangled skein; Only when the mind is settled will there be the moment of opening.
If one applies even the slightest force incorrectly, One will be entangled for ten thousand kalpas with no end in sight.
Chapter Twenty-Eight.
Day and night, with no fixed end, they take things as real; A slight discrepancy and they fall into strife.
Who knows that once one has entered the path to the underworld, One regrets having spent one’s life in bitter enmity?
Chapter Twenty-nine.
The Iron-Faced Yama shows no leniency; Pounding, burning, grinding, and crushing are truly difficult to endure.
If one were to look from the side of the Mirror of Karma, One would never see a good person within the hells.
Chapter Thirty.
Long ensnared in the mire, they have not yet returned; the turbid forms of their bodies are difficult to cleanse at the Western River.
May they one day realize the vow of Bodhi, and the wondrous flowers of the iron tree shall bloom everywhere.
Chapter Thirty-One.
Graveyards are arrayed beneath Mount Beimang; Wild weeds entangle as strange birds cry out.
Long they lie within the spring chambers, never to wake again; Peaches wither and plums fall, past the Qingming festival.
(Chapter Thirty-Two)
The Sutra on the Wondrous Paramitas Spoken by the Buddha Without peer for a thousand ages past, nor to be equaled hereafter;
May humans and spirits alike attain transcendence; Its merit is like heaven, beyond compare.
An Excerpt.
A section from the *Lǚ Zǔshī Sānpǐn Jīng* explaining the origins of the Buddhist teachings, intended to manifest the true Dharma-treasure of this scripture:

"The Pure Subtlety (Qīngwēi) school of Buddhist teaching originated in the vast kalpas. Contemplating emptiness through emptiness, it is void, non-substantial, and quiescent. In the past, there was a Perfected Being."
He was named Dīpaṃkara. Appearing in the middle period, he turned the Great Wheel of Dharma, teaching, transforming, and delivering immeasurable sentient beings;
thus the transmission of the Buddhas first flourished. Subsequently, another Buddha appeared, titled Śākyamuni. From the Tuṣita Heaven, he descended his spirit into Jambudvīpa.
At that time, during the year of the Tiger month under King Zhou Zhao, there was the kingdom of Kapilavastu in Western India.
Its ruler was named Śuddhodana. On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Prince was born, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Due to his long-standing vow, he renounced his kingdom to cultivate the Way. For six years in the Snowy Mountains, he engaged in profound contemplation and ascetic practices;

a magpie built its nest upon his head, and creepers grew through his knees and shins. On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, beholding the rising morning star, he attained sudden enlightenment and became endowed with the six supernormal powers.

Bearing the strength of a dragon-elephant, he opened the way for the future and continued the work of the past. He propagated the Teaching in the Western Regions, beginning at the Deer Park and subsequently at the Jeta Grove.
As golden sand was spread upon the ground, the Buddha-dharma flourished. For forty-nine years, his manifestations and transformations were manifold. At that time, there were bhikṣus...
Together with bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—numbering several thousand—they all listened to the Dharma together, and there was none who did not attain deliverance.
Among them was Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom; the Buddha had frequently relied upon him to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma.

There was a great disciple named Mahākāśyapa, who received the Buddha’s seal of mind and transmitted the orthodox lineage of the Buddha. The Buddha personally bestowed upon him a prediction of his future attainment;
he is thus regarded as the First Patriarch. Furthermore, there was a disciple named Ānanda, foremost among those of vast learning.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he transmitted the Buddhist scriptures and disseminated them throughout the human world. The Buddhist canon of today consists entirely of what he proclaimed. This tradition continued down to Bodhidharma.
By means of great supernormal powers, he subdued the demons and heterodox practitioners of thirty-six locations in a single night.

Having established a vast and solemn vow, he traveled from West India across the sands of the Ganges River to Jambudvīpa in the south, where he preached the Dharma, expounded the teachings, and fully unfolded the school of the Gate of the Patriarchs.
He was granted the secret instructions, attaining them through transcendent awakening. He clarified his mind and beheld his nature; there is nothing much to the Buddha-dharma.

Having swept away everything, he realized his original nature through a single phrase or a solitary word. As for all cleverness, learning, and intellectual knowledge, he set them aside and did not concern himself with them.

Vast and profound, silent and still—this is the leaning toward the fundamental principle. Awakening to the conditions of the Truth, there is nothing that is not non-existent; emptiness is the emptiness of nothingness.
Contemplating this mind within, it is like the limit of space, like the moon in a thousand rivers, like a mirror, like a bubble, and like fragrance within a flower.

Thus it is the emptiness of emptiness; because there is no "non-existence" through which to be empty, there is nothing to grasp. The wondrousness of this single word penetrates all without obstruction:

before, there is no "non-existence" preceding; after, there is no "non-existence" following. It does not arise from hearing or seeing; its profound vision transcends the fleeting. Let all seeing and hearing take their course.
Dejected and self-effacing, he attained the state of causelessness through the very nature of causes and conditions; thus, the Chan school flourished.

Furthermore, throughout successive dynasties, there were many great Dharma Masters who were versed in the Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras; they drew from the great treasury of the Dharma, elucidated and translated its written expressions, and excavated its subtle essence.
It was transmitted throughout all the Jambudvīpa worlds of the trichiliocosm for the sake of sentient beings at large.

It expounds immeasurable causes to dissolve the fever of all afflictions and transform them into a realm of cool serenity; it uproots all suffering and distress, and delivers one from the perils of the burning house.

It rescues all souls in the dark realms and liberates those in the hells, transforming the six paths of existence so that they may attain the bliss of devas and humans, providing inexhaustible benefit and reliance. Thus, the Elephant Teachings...

It has been propagated for a long time, yet its true purport has remained unheard. Among the monastic community, none have attained the authentic transmission. They plunder from east to west, making mere words their primary concern;

they confront one another with sharp mental sparks and vie for supremacy through verbal dexterity. What is called "Chan" should instead expound the esoteric scriptures, recognize the original face, and eschew all superficial ornamentation.
If one investigates the current malpractice, it will bring harm to future generations, causing them to lose their way and become alienated from the truth.
The School: Successive masters have emerged from their former abodes and entered the state of non-being.
Vast and adrift, they have followed the "wild fox Chan," becoming deluded and perverse, reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs while posing as great spiritual authorities.

Even more extreme, they are errant and ignorant, transmitting errors as truth and perpetuating those errors through tradition. As for our Buddha, the Tathāgata—what dharma is there among all dharmas? This is to investigate the source.
Because the fundamental root is empty, all phenomena are void; thus, written characters cannot be established.

It is not that characters are to be discarded, but rather, fearing that future students might seek the truth within the characters and thereby obscure and lose the fundamental root, one sets aside the characters. Yet how could one know that it is truly difficult to discard them entirely?

As for those who discard the characters, what stream do they follow? They merely cling to the characters and form conceptualizations based on them, seeking the Buddha through words and investigating the Buddhist scriptures through texts.
The essential point is this: to deviate from the truth and lose the fundamental tenet is an obstacle of words; this indeed harms the Way.

Furthermore, may you, O Benevolent One, realize that this sutra is the Buddha’s seal of the mind, transmitted through successive generations for the sake of all beings. Expound the Dharma extensively so that they may attain understanding and realization.
Even those of inferior capacity, who are ignorant and obscured by darkness, shall rely on this sutra to repent; thus, you will cause these people to give rise to reverence.

Chant and recite this with the mind morning and evening. After a long time, clarity may arise; one will comprehend the nature of birth and death, exert oneself in various wholesome deeds, and escape the realms of saṃsāra.

Or, by awakening to the *bodhicitta*, one will transcend all higher vehicles. It is not enough merely to recite it verbally; if one lacks a heart of repentance and realization, one can still have sins forgiven.
Even if one relies solely on verbal recitation, one will obtain benefit. When reciting it, one should give rise to great joy, chanting it aloud and clearly.

I praise it. May all sentient beings of both the hidden and manifest realms, including demons, heterodox species, and the lingering remnants of deceased spirits, upon hearing this sutra, universally receive its benefits and all be delivered across the sea of suffering.
This is not to say that merely reciting this sutra with the mouth is sufficient;
one must lack no heart of upholding and receiving, no heart of reverence, no heart of sincere faith, no heart of exultation, no heart of impartial benefit, and no heart of selflessness.
They merely recite the scriptures and thereby claim to obtain merit. From day to day, as the days pass, they decline and decay.
All the Buddhist scriptures are treated as mere means for food and clothing; those who recite the scriptures seek after empty words, and those who perform the recitation respond with empty words.
Because all sentient beings rely on empty words, they hold this scripture in light esteem, and thus the teachings of the Buddhas have nothing remaining.

One must know that this sutra possesses great liberation; it transforms all restlessness like the "Guangling San" melody, transforms all afflictions like a *maṇi* jewel, ferries those drowning across like a Prajñā boat, produces all nourishment like the *pāramitās*, and illuminates all deep darkness like a lamp in a lacquered room.
Possessing these various kinds of immeasurable benefits, one should simply compose this text.
[These] characters are merely crude and erroneous; they are like dregs that can never be relied upon. For this reason, the Chan school, being aware of such things, sweeps them all away.

They settle their minds in internal contemplation, emptying both internal and external appearances, sitting in silent stillness, and taking up the lead of a single inquiry to investigate the ultimate purport.
There is a sweeping away even of emptiness; since there is nothing to be emptied, through this absence of emptiness, one then realizes this.
The Essential Meaning: If one stays in a dark room and raises a single flaming torch, there is nothing that is not seen and nothing that is not illuminated;

there is no obstruction whatsoever. Because there is no obstruction, it is entrusted to you for exposition. It is complete with Heaven, coexistent with Heaven and Earth, neither confined by things nor existing as a thing—this is called the *Brahman*.
When the incense smoke of the *Brahman* rises, the realms of the hidden and the manifest are harmonized; this is what is meant.
Chan. The principles of Chan are profound and subtle; both devas and humans have thoroughly investigated them. Those who have fully mastered their essential meaning possess the seed of Buddha-bodhi.
It is thus, it is thus. Such is the great purport of the Westward Transmission. When one contemplates in this manner, the Buddha-dharma is complete.
